item.title: Listening Log to Stanley Myers – Cavatina
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: I found the combination of two acoustic guitars and orchestra interesting, especially because of the relationship between the guitars and the strings. Together, they create a romantic and intimate atmosphere. I particularly like the contrast...
item.content:encoded:
I found the combination of two acoustic guitars and orchestra interesting, especially because of the relationship between the guitars and the strings. Together, they create a romantic and intimate atmosphere. I particularly like the contrast between the clear attack of the guitars and the warmer sound of the strings.

I was also interested in how the two guitars explore different registers. At some moments, they reach very high and low registers at the same time, creating a wide sound space. However, I sometimes felt that having two guitars did not add enough to the original musical idea. The piece was originally written for one guitar, and for me, the simplicity of the single guitar is part of what makes Cavatina effective.

If two guitars are used, I would expect more interaction between them, such as one guitar taking over the melody or the two instruments creating a stronger dialogue. I also think there could be more exploration of different guitar techniques or textures.

item.title: Listening Log – Élégie Op. 24 (Gabriel Fauré)
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: At the beginning of Fauré’s Élégie, I hear something almost like a slow march. The piano creates the feeling of heavy, dragging steps before the cello enters with the main melody. When the cello begins, the...
item.content:encoded:
At the beginning of Fauré’s Élégie, I hear something almost like a slow march. The piano creates the feeling of heavy, dragging steps before the cello enters with the main melody. When the cello begins, the mood becomes much more clearly sad. I particularly notice how the cello suspensions create tension.

In the middle section, both instruments become more active and the texture feels almost “fuzzy” to me. There is then a surprising change of mood. The piano becomes more playful and energetic, taking a stronger role, while the cello seems to hold on to the sadness of the opening. It feels almost as if the cello is pushing against the piano’s new energy.

Eventually, the cello seems to give in and follows the piano into this more energetic section. The two instruments begin to sound almost like they are having a conversation, responding to each other. When the main motif returns, it is more energetic than at the beginning, but the piece does not end happily. Instead, it returns to a calm and dark atmosphere. I like this because the sadness seems to remain present even after the music has changed.

item.title: Listening to Camille Saint-Saëns- The Swan
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: At first, The Swan sounds like a very gentle and beautiful piece. I particularly like how a minor note appears in the melody and suddenly changes the feeling of the music. It brings a small sense of...
item.content:encoded:
At first, The Swan sounds like a very gentle and beautiful piece. I particularly like how a minor note appears in the melody and suddenly changes the feeling of the music. It brings a small sense of sadness or fragility to an otherwise peaceful melody. I think this contrast makes the piece more interesting and prevents it from sounding simply sweet.

The cello, performed by Yo-Yo Ma, and the piano, performed by Kathryn Stott, work very closely together to create the image of a swan moving through the water. The long, smooth lines of the cello make it sound almost as if the swan is singing. The piano has a different role, providing the movement and harmonic support underneath the melody. I especially like the moments when the cello moves upwards while the piano moves downwards. This creates a beautiful sense of expansion and movement between the two instruments.

Towards the end, I really like the way the piano becomes more sparkling and active. For me, it creates an image of the swan shining in the sunlight. The piece therefore feels almost like a small musical picture: the cello represents the swan itself, while the piano creates the water, light, and movement around it.

item.title: Listening to Alanis Morissette – You Oughta Know
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: I have been listening to this song for thirty years. I knew it was raw. I knew it was angry. But I never stopped to look at who played on it until recently, and that...
item.content:encoded:
I have been listening to this song for thirty years. I knew it was raw. I knew it was angry. But I never stopped to look at who played on it until recently, and that changed everything about how I hear it.

The lyrics are almost confrontational in their specificity. There is no attempt to disguise the target, no softening for the listener’s comfort. That directness is what made the song feel so real in 1995 and still makes it feel real now. You believe her completely. Whether it is autobiographical or not almost doesn’t matter, because it sounds like it costs her something to sing it.

But this time I was listening differently, because I had just discovered that the bass and guitar were recorded by Flea and Dave Navarro. Two musicians I love, playing on a song I already loved, and I had no idea. Flea’s bass is the thing that gives the track its body. It moves constantly, it has that low-end urgency. And Navarro’s guitar sits underneath everything, restrained, almost uncomfortable, which is exactly right for the song.

What it made me think about was how much a player’s identity can come through even when they are in service of someone else’s work. I didn’t know it was Flea. But I felt something in that bass that I couldn’t name. It turns out it was just him, being himself.

item.title: Listening to Claude Debussy – Nocturne (L. 82)
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: I was researching early Debussy, trying to understand how he got from where he started to where he ended up, and this piece appeared. The opening is slow and loose, almost like the pianist is...
item.content:encoded:
I was researching early Debussy, trying to understand how he got from where he started to where he ended up, and this piece appeared.

The opening is slow and loose, almost like the pianist is still deciding what to play. There’s no dramatic entry. It just begins, gently, and I found myself relaxing without noticing. The melody drifts more than it moves forward, and somehow that’s enough to hold my attention.

What I wasn’t prepared for was the middle section. Something shifts. The texture thickens, the dynamic rises, and the piece feels urgent. It surprised me. And then it passes. The calm returns, the melody comes back, and the piece closes as gently as it opened.

By the end I felt like I’d been let in on something private. Not a grand statement. Just a mood, carefully held.

item.title: Listening to Mykola Leontovych – Dudaryk
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: Analysing this piece provides a good contrast to the contemporary works I’ve examined. Performed by the O. Koshetz Choir, this a cappella choral piece demonstrates how the human voice alone can create a complex narrative structure...
item.content:encoded:
Analysing this piece provides a good contrast to the contemporary works I’ve examined. Performed by the O. Koshetz Choir, this a cappella choral piece demonstrates how the human voice alone can create a complex narrative structure and emotional arc.

The piece starts with a simple, rhythmic motive that mimics the sound of a piper’s pipe. This motive acts as a leitmotif, recurring throughout to maintain the connection to the titular character. The build-up is achieved through increasing rhythmic complexity and a broadening of the choral harmony, moving from a transparent, light texture to a much denser, more resonant one.

The piece feels like a celebration of folk life, yet it’s also grounded in intensity. The timbre of the choir shifts from playful and light in the initial verses to a powerful resonance in the climactic sections. The way the different vocal lines intertwine feels like a “reflective mosaic” of people coming together, each adding their own color to the collective whole.

It reminds me that even without external instruments or a dedicated narrator, the human voice can convey a powerful sense of story and emotion. This has given me much to think about in terms of how I might use choral elements or even just layered vocal textures in my own project.

item.title: Listening to Marcello – Concerto for oboe and strings Adagio in D minor
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: The opening dissonance of Marcello’s Oboe Concerto is one of the things I find most interesting. It creates a small moment of tension that does not seem to predict the beautiful melody that follows. This makes the...
item.content:encoded:
The opening dissonance of Marcello’s Oboe Concerto is one of the things I find most interesting. It creates a small moment of tension that does not seem to predict the beautiful melody that follows. This makes the entrance of the oboe feel even more expressive.

For me, the oboe sounds almost like a singer. Its melody moves up and down in a way that reminds me of someone crying or trying to express something difficult. This makes the piece feel very sad and emotional. The oboe has a very direct and human quality.

I also notice the repeated movement of the strings underneath the melody. They seem to be constantly moving forward, but slowly, almost like dragging their feet. This creates a dark and somber atmosphere that remains present through much of the piece. I find this interesting because the oboe melody itself is beautiful and lyrical, while the string accompaniment is more repetitive and restrained.

This contrast between the expressive melody and the repetitive background is, for me, one of the strongest aspects of the piece. The strings create a continuous emotional environment while the oboe seems to speak or cry above it. The simplicity of the accompaniment gives the oboe space, allowing the melody to carry most of the emotional weight.

item.title: Listening to Arvo Pärt – Spiegel im Spiegel
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: I listened to Spiegel im Spiegel in versions for violin, viola, and cello. I preferred the cello version because I think its darker timbre creates a stronger contrast with the high and soft sound of the piano....
item.content:encoded:
I listened to Spiegel im Spiegel in versions for violin, viola, and cello. I preferred the cello version because I think its darker timbre creates a stronger contrast with the high and soft sound of the piano. The piece feels very solemn and simple. Although there is a piano, I hear the string instrument almost as the main character, while the piano creates a kind of musical landscape around it. It provides the harmonic space without taking the main focus.

At some moments, the piece reminds me of a lullaby. I particularly like the way Pärt uses the piano’s lower notes. They appear at carefully chosen moments and can create a feeling of arrival or ending. However, the higher piano notes continue, and the string instrument follows them. Because of this, the music never completely settles. There is always a sense of continuation.

This relates to Pärt’s style of using simplicity, repetition, and silence as important musical elements. I read the phrase “the composer who made silence sing”, and I can understand this idea in Spiegel im Spiegel. There is not complete silence in the piece, but a strong sense of quietness is always present. The spaces between the notes become almost as important as the notes themselves.

item.title: Listening to Rosalía, Carminho – Memória
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: The global success of Rosalía’s new album, Lux, made it impossible for me to ignore, so I finally sat down to listen. In my view, the record is a triumph because it is a conceptual...
item.content:encoded:
The global success of Rosalía’s new album, Lux, made it impossible for me to ignore, so I finally sat down to listen. In my view, the record is a triumph because it is a conceptual work where a mainstream artist takes the liberty to create something entirely different from the formatted pop we hear today. Among the tracks, Memória stood out most. Partly because I am Portuguese and I adore Carminho, but also because of how it bridges two worlds.

To me, Memória captures a deep sense of saudade through its inherent sadness. The dramatic contrast between the quiet instruments and the intense, longing delivery of the lyrics creates a mood of profound introspection. It feels like a bridge between the past and the present, where the minimalist production allows the emotional weight of the Fado tradition to shine without being over-produced. I found the experience deeply moving, as it proves that mainstream music can still be surprising.

I adore how the minimalist texture, featuring a delicate interplay between harp and piano, replaces the traditional Portuguese guitar, pushing the sound toward an ethereal, dreamlike atmosphere rather than a standard folk style.

item.title: Listening Log to Rachmaninoff – Piano Concerto No.2, Op.18: II. Adagio sostenuto
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: The flute and clarinet conversation at the beginning is one of the things I find most beautiful about this movement. They seem to answer and complete each other’s phrases, while the piano is initially very...
item.content:encoded:
The flute and clarinet conversation at the beginning is one of the things I find most beautiful about this movement. They seem to answer and complete each other’s phrases, while the piano is initially very minimal and almost stays in the background. When the piano becomes more present, it feels as if it pushes the two instruments towards a fuller and more complete version of the melody. I really like how this transition happens so naturally.

It is surprising how the music then develops from this romantic and gentle melody into something much more passionate and intense. In the middle section, the piano becomes the dominant force, with a powerful and dramatic sound that almost completely covers the orchestra. Although the music becomes darker in the solo, I do not hear it only as sadness. For me, it feels more like a kind of burning love or emotional intensity that has become impossible to contain.
